questions.q: What does a public group grant on its own, with no sharing rule, manual share, or other mechanism pointing at it?
options: Nothing — a public group has no access level or visibility implication by itself; it only matters once something else targets it
Read Only access to every object in the org
Automatic membership in the role hierarchy
Ownership of every record owned by its members
questions.explain: A public group is purely a reusable, named collection of users (or roles, or other groups). It grants nothing by itself — its value comes entirely from being a target that sharing rules, manual shares, and folder access point at.

questions.q: Public group 'Team A' contains public group 'Team B' as a nested member. A sharing rule grants access to Team A. Who actually receives that access?
options: Only the users added directly to Team A, not anyone in Team B
Only the users in Team B, since nested groups override the outer group
Every user transitively reachable through Team A, including everyone in nested Team B
No one, since sharing rules cannot target a group that contains nested groups
questions.explain: A sharing rule targeting a group with nested members grants access to everyone transitively reachable through every layer of nesting — which is exactly why nested groups create an audit challenge: the true population isn't visible from the sharing rule alone.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe group nesting as a real audit risk for an architect to manage?
options: Because nested groups are deprecated and will stop working in a future release
Because a change to a nested sub-group's membership silently changes who every sharing rule pointed at the outer group actually reaches, with no notification
Because nested groups can only be created by a system administrator profile
Because nesting is only supported on custom objects, not standard objects
questions.explain: Someone adding a user to a nested sub-group silently expands access for every sharing rule (or other mechanism) pointed at any outer group containing that sub-group, with nothing surfacing that this happened — which is why reviewing nesting depth and current membership matters.

questions.q: A batch of inbound Leads is assigned to a shared queue with three members. How does record access work for those Leads before anyone takes ownership?
options: No one can see the Leads until an admin manually shares them
Only the queue's creator can see the Leads
Every queue member automatically has access to every Lead currently assigned to the queue, simply by being a member
Access depends on each member's individual role in the hierarchy, not on queue membership
questions.explain: Because a queue effectively stands in as the record's owner, every member of that queue automatically and implicitly has access to everything currently sitting in the queue — this doesn't require a separate sharing rule.

questions.q: A Lead sitting in a shared queue is taken by one of the queue's members, becoming that member's individually owned record. What happens to the other queue members' access to that specific Lead?
options: It's unaffected — they retain the same access they had while it was in the queue
It disappears, since the record is no longer owned by the queue and implicit queue access no longer applies to it
It upgrades automatically to Read/Write for all former queue members
The Lead is automatically returned to the queue after 24 hours
questions.explain: Implicit queue access exists only while the queue itself owns the record. Once an individual member takes ownership, the record leaves the queue's ownership and the other members' implicit access goes with it, unless some other mechanism (a sharing rule, a team) grants it separately.
